title: Robotics
tagline: Rigid-body motions, forward and inverse kinematics, Jacobians, manipulator dynamics, trajectory planning, motion and force control, mobile robots and motion planning
summary: Robots are mechanisms under computer control. The course describes rigid-body motion with rotation matrices and homogeneous transformations, solves the forward and inverse kinematics of manipulators, derives velocity Jacobians and singularities, formulates manipulator dynamics, plans trajectories, designs joint-space, task-space and force controllers, and introduces mobile robots, perception and motion planning.
overview: A robot arm is a mechanism whose joints are driven by motors under computer control, and a mobile robot is a vehicle that must work out where it is before it can decide where to go. Both rest on the same small set of ideas: the position and orientation of a rigid body are described by a $4\times4$ homogeneous transformation; the geometry of a robot is a function from joint variables to such transformations; its velocities are related by a Jacobian matrix; its motion obeys Lagrange's or Newton–Euler's equations; and a controller closes the loop around sensors that are never perfect.

The course follows that chain. It starts with rotation matrices, exponential coordinates, Euler angles, unit quaternions and homogeneous transformations, then builds the forward kinematics of serial manipulators with Denavit–Hartenberg parameters and the product-of-exponentials formula. Inverse kinematics is solved in closed form for the planar arm and for six-axis arms with a spherical wrist, and numerically by Newton–Raphson and damped least squares. The Jacobian links joint rates to end-effector velocities and, by the principle of virtual work, end-effector forces to joint torques; its singularities and manipulability ellipsoids explain where a robot is weak. Manipulator dynamics, trajectory generation, and motion, impedance and force control follow. The last two chapters move to wheeled robots — nonholonomic constraints, odometry and path following — and to configuration-space motion planning, sensing and Kalman filtering.

Two habits make the subject manageable. The first is to be explicit about frames: every vector and transform carries the names of the frames it relates, and most errors in robotics software are frame errors. The second is to test every formula on a robot small enough to check by hand — the planar two-link arm appears in nearly every chapter for that reason. The prerequisites are rigid-body kinematics and kinetics from [[dynamics]], mobility and linkage analysis from [[mechanisms]], and feedback control from [[control-systems]]; the linear algebra (matrix exponentials, eigenvalues, the singular value decomposition, least squares) is taught in Maths Atlas.
outcomes: Represent orientations and poses with rotation matrices, exponential coordinates, Euler angles, unit quaternions and homogeneous transformations, and convert between them.
Assign Denavit–Hartenberg frames to a serial manipulator and compute its forward kinematics, and derive the same map with the product-of-exponentials formula.
Solve the inverse kinematics of planar arms and of six-axis arms with a spherical wrist in closed form, and apply Newton–Raphson and damped-least-squares iterations to general arms.
Derive the geometric Jacobian, locate singular configurations, and compute manipulability and the joint torques that balance an end-effector force.
Formulate the equations of motion of a serial manipulator with the Euler–Lagrange and recursive Newton–Euler methods and use their structural properties.
Design point-to-point, via-point and Cartesian trajectories with polynomial and trapezoidal time scalings that respect velocity and acceleration limits.
Design and analyse independent-joint PID, PD-plus-gravity, computed-torque, impedance and hybrid position/force controllers.
Model wheeled mobile robots with nonholonomic constraints, compute odometry and design a path-following controller.
Plan collision-free paths in configuration space with graph search and sampling-based planners, and fuse noisy sensor data with Bayes and Kalman filters.

chapters.title: Rigid-body motions and transformations
chapters.summary: Rotation matrices, Euler angles, quaternions and homogeneous transformations.

chapters.title: Forward kinematics
chapters.summary: Joint variables, Denavit–Hartenberg parameters and the product-of-exponentials formula.

chapters.title: Inverse kinematics
chapters.summary: Analytical and numerical solutions of the inverse kinematics, multiple solutions and workspaces.

chapters.title: Velocity kinematics and Jacobians
chapters.summary: The manipulator Jacobian, singularities, manipulability, and the relation between joint torques and end-effector forces.

chapters.title: Manipulator dynamics
chapters.summary: The Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler equations of motion of robot arms.

chapters.title: Trajectory planning
chapters.summary: Point-to-point and path trajectories in joint and task space, polynomial and spline profiles, and time scaling.

chapters.title: Motion and force control
chapters.summary: Independent-joint PID control, computed-torque control, task-space control, and impedance and force control.

chapters.title: Mobile robots
chapters.summary: Kinematics of wheeled robots, odometry, and the basics of localisation and mapping.

chapters.title: Motion planning and perception
chapters.summary: Configuration space, sampling-based motion planners, and sensing for robots with cameras and lidar.

history.title: Euler's rotation theorem
history.detail: Leonhard Euler shows that any displacement of a rigid body with one point fixed is a rotation about an axis through that point — the basis of axis–angle and exponential coordinates.

history.title: Quaternions
history.detail: William Rowan Hamilton discovers the quaternions; unit quaternions are now the standard singularity-free representation of orientation in robot and attitude software.

history.title: Denavit–Hartenberg notation
history.detail: Jacques Denavit and Richard Hartenberg publish a matrix notation for lower-pair mechanisms in the Journal of Applied Mechanics, describing each joint–link pair with four parameters.

history.title: First industrial robot at work
history.detail: A Unimate, designed by George Devol and commercialised by Joseph Engelberger's Unimation, unloads a die-casting press at General Motors' Ternstedt plant in Trenton, New Jersey.

history.title: Closed-form inverse kinematics
history.detail: Donald Pieper's Stanford thesis shows that six-axis arms with three intersecting wrist axes have inverse kinematics solvable in closed form, the design rule followed by most industrial arms since.

history.title: The Stanford Arm
history.detail: Victor Scheinman builds a six-axis, all-electric, computer-controlled arm at the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; its design line led through Vicarm to Unimation's PUMA.

history.title: Recursive Newton–Euler dynamics
history.detail: Luh, Walker and Paul publish a recursive Newton–Euler scheme whose cost grows linearly with the number of links, making computed-torque control feasible in real time.

history.title: Impedance control
history.detail: Neville Hogan's three-part paper argues that a manipulator in contact should control the relation between motion and force — its mechanical impedance — rather than either alone.

history.title: Probabilistic roadmaps
history.detail: Kavraki, Švestka, Latombe and Overmars publish the probabilistic roadmap planner, making motion planning practical for robots with many degrees of freedom.

history.title: Rapidly-exploring random trees
history.detail: Steven LaValle introduces the RRT, a sampling-based planner that grows a tree from the start configuration and became the basis of many single-query planners.

references.title: Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control
references.authors: K. M. Lynch and F. C. Park
references.note: Cambridge University Press. Screw theory, exponential coordinates and the product-of-exponentials formula from the start; a free preprint and videos accompany it.

references.title: Robot Modeling and Control
references.authors: M. W. Spong, S. Hutchinson and M. Vidyasagar
references.note: Wiley, 2nd edition. The standard undergraduate text for Denavit–Hartenberg kinematics, Jacobians, Lagrangian dynamics and independent-joint and computed-torque control; the conventions of this course follow it.

references.title: Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control
references.note: Pearson, 4th edition. Clear worked treatment of frames, kinematics and Newton–Euler dynamics; uses the modified Denavit–Hartenberg convention.

references.title: Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control
references.authors: B. Siciliano, L. Sciavicco, L. Villani and G. Oriolo
references.note: Springer. Thorough on differential kinematics, redundancy, trajectory planning and interaction (force and impedance) control.

references.title: A Mathematical Introduction to Robotic Manipulation
references.authors: R. M. Murray, Z. Li and S. S. Sastry
references.note: CRC Press. The rigorous Lie-group treatment of rigid motions, twists and wrenches; for readers who want the proofs behind the exponential coordinates.

references.title: Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms
references.note: Springer. Spatial vector algebra and the recursive algorithms (Newton–Euler, articulated-body) used in simulators and controllers.

references.title: Planning Algorithms
references.note: Cambridge University Press (also free online). Configuration space, graph search and sampling-based planning in depth.

references.title: Probabilistic Robotics
references.authors: S. Thrun, W. Burgard and D. Fox
references.note: MIT Press. Bayes, Kalman and particle filters for localisation and mapping.

references.title: Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots
references.authors: R. Siegwart, I. R. Nourbakhsh and D. Scaramuzza
references.note: MIT Press, 2nd edition. Wheeled-robot kinematics, sensors, perception and navigation at an introductory level.
